workTitle: Prelude in D-flat major, Op. 28 No. 15

clues.label: A musical characteristic
clues.text: One note just keeps tapping through almost the whole piece, hopping from hand to hand. The music slips into the minor, gets darker, then finds its way home.

clues.label: A place the composer worked
clues.text: Winter 1838-39: a half-abandoned monastery on a Mediterranean island. Non-stop rain. The composer is getting sicker. The neighbors won't come near — they think the house has consumption. And the piano they shipped over sits in customs for weeks.

clues.label: A biographical detail
clues.text: Born near Warsaw in 1810. Left home at twenty and never went back. In a foreign capital he made his living teaching and playing in salons, almost never in big public concerts.

clues.label: A relationship with a contemporary
clues.text: He was living with the novelist who published as George Sand — she planned this disastrous winter trip. And after he died, they took his heart back to Warsaw and sealed it in a church pillar. If you know one piano composer, it's this guy.

explanation.summary: Rain, a sick winter on an island, and George Sand: Frédéric Chopin (Fryderyk), writing in Spain at the charterhouse of Valldemossa on Mallorca, 1838-39.

points.text: [PLACEHOLDER] Commentary on the manuscript hand goes here once a real autograph scan replaces the placeholder image.
That stubborn repeated A-flat — which turns into G-sharp when the piece goes minor — is why people still call this the "Raindrop" prelude.
The island is Mallorca and the monastery is Valldemossa, where he finished the Op. 28 Preludes. Spain is the answer only because his health dragged him there.
Warsaw, then a one-way trip to Paris. That's his story — even though this particular piece was written far from both.
George Sand plus the heart in the Warsaw pillar. That's Chopin, and her Un hiver à Majorque is literally this winter.
